The newly hatched chicks are precocial and emerge with a wet body mass averaging 44 grams [Wwb = 44 grams], a modest starting weight that reflects the limited yolk reserves available at hatching. This initial mass is a critical factor in early survival, as heavier hatchlings generally possess greater energy stores to sustain them during the first days of independent foraging. Field observations suggest that the timing of hatching is tightly synchronized with local invertebrate emergence, ensuring that abundant food resources are available when the brood begins its active feeding phase and enabling the young to exploit the seasonal pulse of prey abundance that drives early growth.

Only one clutch is laid per year [F_R_i = one clutch is laid per year], a reproductive strategy that prioritizes a large, single brood over multiple smaller attempts. This high fecundity per event is typical of many duck species that experience significant nest predation, as laying a large clutch can compensate for potential losses during the incubation period. This relatively high metabolic rate is consistent with the species' active foraging lifestyle and its reliance on diving to capture submerged prey. The measurement was obtained from post-absorptive adults during the resting phase of their circadian cycle, ensuring that the recorded value represents true basal conditions. Such metabolic data are essential for constructing accurate energy budgets and for understanding how this species allocates resources between self-maintenance and reproductive effort over the course of its life.

Newly laid eggs have an initial wet weight of 66 grams [Ww0 = 66 grams], representing a considerable maternal investment relative to the female's own body mass. The interplay between size dimorphism and lifespan is a subject of ongoing interest, as the slightly larger males do not exhibit a significantly different survival rate from females, suggesting that any costs associated with larger body size in this species are relatively minor.
